strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and increasingly important problem: the growing IO/memory bottleneck in fine-grained, sparse MoE training as models trend toward higher granularity and sparsity (well supported by Table 1's survey of real frontier models).

Technically deep and novel kernel-level contributions: memory-efficient backward algorithm (avoiding caching Y, dY, dO_e) that provably matches the activation memory of a dense model with equivalent activated parameters, plus detailed Hopper/Blackwell-specific overlap strategies (Ping-Pong scheduling, TMA vs cp.async gather/scatter tradeoffs, tensor memory usage on Blackwell).

Extensive and carefully controlled empirical evaluation: comparisons against many strong baselines (ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, DeepGEMM/DeepGEMM++) across model scales from 1.4B to 685B, with both synthetic and real open-source model configurations (Figure 15), and detailed component-level ablations (Appendix E) isolating the effect of gather fusion, epilogue fusion, scatter vs TMA store, and top-K kernel design.

Novel token rounding (TR) routing algorithm is theoretically clean (bounded to a single tile deviation from top-K) and empirically validated for quality preservation across multiple model scales and sparsity regimes (0.5B-1.8B), with thorough ablations on rounding subroutine, microbatch size, and tile size sensitivity.

Demonstrates real end-to-end training throughput gains (213B vs 225B tokens/day using appreciably fewer GPUs, 64 vs 96 H100s) rather than only synthetic kernel microbenchmarks, improving practical credibility.
Open-sourced kernels and codebase, and very detailed appendices (notation tables, algorithmic pseudocode, benchmark configs) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Token rounding's quality preservation is only validated at relatively small scales (up to 1.8B parameters, ≤100B tokens), while the throughput benchmarks are shown at much larger configurations (7B-685B); it remains unclear whether TR's quality-preservation guarantees extend to production-scale training runs matching the kernel throughput experiments.

The headline end-to-end comparison (213B tokens/day on 64 H100s for SonicMoE vs 225B tokens/day on 96 H100s for ScatterMoE) uses different GPU counts, and while the authors frame this favorably, a matched-hardware comparison would make the throughput claim more directly interpretable.

The paper is systems/kernel-engineering heavy with substantial low-level GPU architecture detail (CUTLASS, TMA, warpgroups, tensor memory); this may be less accessible or evaluable by a general AI audience and could be a better fit for a systems-focused venue, even though the topic is highly relevant to efficient LLM training.

Token rounding is fundamentally a training-time approximation (not usable directly at inference without switching back to TC), and the paper does not deeply explore robustness of this train/inference mismatch beyond the small-scale experiments, nor its interaction with expert-parallel deployment settings.

Given the complexity of the described kernel engineering, exact reproducibility for non-specialist readers may be challenging despite code release, and some comparisons (e.g., DeepGEMM++ being an in-house extension of DeepGEMM) may not be independently verifiable baselines.

Limited discussion of how the approach interacts with expert-parallel communication overlap (mentioned only as future work), which is important for very large-scale training where all-to-all costs often dominate.

strengths: Comprehensive systems contribution spanning three complementary techniques: a memory-efficient MoE backward algorithm, IO-aware kernel design (gather/epilogue fusion, Ping-Pong scheduling on Hopper and TMEM-based overlap on Blackwell), and a novel tile-aware token rounding routing method — each independently useful and well-motivated by a clear arithmetic-intensity analysis.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of model scales (1.4B to 685B-parameter configurations matching real open-source MoE architectures like DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-Next, Kimi-Linear, gpt-oss), and across two GPU generations (H100 and B300), with detailed kernel-level runtime breakdowns.
Strong, credible real end-to-end training throughput validation using FSDP-2 on 64-96 H100s (213B vs 225B tokens/day) rather than only synthetic microbenchmarks, which substantiates practical impact.

Very thorough ablation studies (appendices F and G) isolating the contribution of gather fusion, epilogue fusion, aggregation strategy, top-K kernel design, and different token-rounding subroutines, and studying sensitivity to microbatch size and tile size.

Token rounding is validated not just for speed but for downstream task quality across multiple model sizes/sparsity regimes (Table 2), with a solid comparison against reasonable alternative baselines (EC with auxiliary router, EC with TC finetuning, token dropping).

Clear, detailed comparison table (Table 1) and appendix discussion (Appendix B) contrasting SonicMoE's design choices against ScatterMoE, MoMoE, MegaBlocks, Megatron, and DeepGEMM, showing careful positioning relative to prior work.
Code and kernels are open-sourced with a permissive license, aiding reproducibility and practical adoption by the community.

Mathematically rigorous derivation showing the proposed dS/dH computation path avoids caching Y/dY without added FLOPs, and clear proof-like guarantees for token rounding's bounded deviation from top-K routing.
weaknesses: The core techniques (gather/epilogue fusion, Ping-Pong overlap of MMA and IO, tile-based token rounding) are largely engineering optimizations and hardware-specific applications of known GEMM-optimization concepts (e.g., from FlashAttention-3) rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas, which may limit the paper's broader intellectual novelty despite its practical value.

Token rounding's quality preservation is only validated on relatively small models (0.5B-1.8B parameters) trained on modest token budgets (20-100B tokens), leaving open whether the reported quality parity holds at the scale of the very large sparse models (100B-1T+ params, trillions of tokens) that motivate the paper's introduction.

Some baselines used for comparison (e.g., "DeepGEMM++") are custom, author-constructed combinations of DeepGEMM with additional hand-written kernels, which, while reasonably justified, are not independently validated as a de facto SOTA baseline and could bias reported speedups favorably.

The paper's writing and presentation is extremely dense, with a very large number of figures/tables and terse notation, which may hinder accessibility and careful independent verification of specific claims despite the extensive appendix.

The token-rounding speedup benefits are concentrated in high-sparsity regimes; for more moderate sparsity settings common in many current models, the gains are comparatively small (e.g., ~2-8% in several configurations in Figure 14), somewhat tempering the practical significance of this specific contribution.

Discussion of low-precision (FP8/MXFP8/MXFP4) training, which is increasingly standard for frontier MoE training, is deferred entirely to future work, leaving a gap regarding the applicability of these optimizations under the precision regimes actually used by the very large models referenced (e.g., DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2).
